facts.fact: As of the June 10, 2024 Federal Register notice, the CFTC stated it had issued two final determinations under 17 CFR 40.11.

On April 2, 2012, the CFTC prohibited Nadex self-certified event contracts on election outcomes from being listed or made available for clearing or trading, finding that they involved gaming and were contrary to the public interest.
The related 90-day review had begun on January 3, 2012.

On June 23, 2023, the CFTC began a 90-day review of self-certified event contracts based on which political party controlled each chamber of Congress, and on September 22, 2023 it issued an order prohibiting those contracts from being listed or made available for clearing or trading as gaming, as activity unlawful under state law, and as contrary to the public interest.
On August 26, 2022, the CFTC began a 90-day review of congressional-control event contracts submitted for approval; the submission was withdrawn before any final determination under 17 CFR 40.11.

Effective February 4, 2026, the CFTC withdrew the June 10, 2024 proposed amendments that would have further specified which event contracts involve gaming and may not be listed, and it said it does not intend to issue final rules on that proposal.

On October 2, 2024, the D.C.
Circuit recorded that the district court had vacated the Commission’s treatment of Congressional Control Contracts as gaming or gambling, and it dissolved the administrative stay of that judgment.

On May 7, 2025, the D.C.
Circuit granted the Commission’s unopposed motion to dismiss the appeal in No.
24-5205 and ordered the mandate issued forthwith to the district court.

The swap-definition proposal issued by the Commission on October 15, 2026, and published October 19, 2026, would expressly include politics-related event contracts as swaps, and written comments are due November 18, 2026.

In that same proposal, the Commission reported that in August 2026 about $11 million of monthly event-contract volume on designated contract markets reporting to the Commission was in politics-related contracts, including elections-related contracts.

CFTC staff, in an FAQ noting a September 24, 2026 addition, said a futures commission merchant relying on Staff Letter 26-05 may apply a customer’s non-security crypto assets deposited as margin in cleared-swaps accounts, and stated that the FAQ creates no enforceable rights.
On October 13, 2026, the Commission published an advanced notice on rules for crypto-asset transactions and markets, with comments due December 14, 2026.

Staff Letter 26-05, reproducing the December 8, 2025 no-action position, limits its relief to staff not recommending enforcement when a futures commission merchant accepts certain non-security digital assets as customer margin collateral or deposits the merchant’s own payment stablecoins as residual interest, and states that customer funds may be held only at banks, trust companies, futures commission merchants, or derivatives clearing organizations.

That same letter states that the no-action position has no effect on Commission Regulation 1.25’s permitted investments of customer funds, is only the Division’s view, and may be conditioned, modified, suspended, or terminated by the Division.
Under 17 CFR 140.99, as amended through September 4, 2024, a no-action letter does not bind the Commission, and only the beneficiary may rely on it.

The current text of 17 CFR 40.11(a) still provides that a registered entity shall not list or clear an excluded-commodity contract that involves gaming or an activity unlawful under state or federal law.

On August 28, 2026, the Ninth Circuit said 17 CFR 40.11 remains in force and bars gaming contracts, and remanded because the district court had not decided whether the exchange’s election contracts, which the court said are illegal under Nevada law, are swaps.

The survey was conducted October 12–19, 2026, via telephone using a random sample of 1,471 likely midterm election voters.
The overall margin of sampling error is +/- 2.81 percentage points.

Republican candidates hold razor-thin advantages in both the Florida governor and U.S.
Senate races, according to the latest statewide poll released Tuesday by the Public Opinion Research Lab at the University of North Florida.
In the gubernatorial contest, Republican Byron Donalds leads Democrat David Jolly by two percentage points, 49% to 47%, with 4% undecided.
Meanwhile, Republican Sen.
Ashley Moody holds a four-point edge, 49% to 45%, against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon in the U.S.
Senate race, with 5% undecided.
Both leads for Republicans have narrowed since UNF's July poll, which showed Donalds ahead by five points and Moody by eight points.
"Though Donalds enjoys a slight advantage, these numbers suggest a competitive gubernatorial race, similar to the race between Andrew Gillum and Ron DeSantis in 2018, which was won by less than a percentage point.
Given the margin of error, a win by either candidate would be unsurprising," said Dr.
Sean Freeder, a UNF political science professor and faculty director of UNF's Public Opinion Research Lab.
Freeder pointed to President Trump's "near-historic" low approval ratings for the close race in Florida.
READ MORE: 2026 Election: Amendments, referendums and other questions on your midterms ballot — a guide
"Donalds' attempt to win over Black voters does not appear to be working, as Donalds receives just 10% of their support, only slightly more than Senator Moody’s 9%, despite not engaging in nearly as much effort," Freeder added.
Cross-party support and independent voters are playing key roles in keeping the margins tight.
Jolly holds a 16-point advantage over Donalds among independents, pulling 11% of registered Republicans compared to Donalds’ 5% among Democrats.
In the U.S.
Senate contest, Nixon leads independents by 15 points.
“Like Donalds, Moody appears to be in a competitive race, though one that leans more decisively in her favor.
Independents favor Nixon by 15 points, and also appear to be more concerned about Moody’s ties to Hope Florida than Nixon’s ties to socialism,” Freeder noted.
“Given the anti-incumbent mood of swing voters, both Donalds and Moody’s success depends upon Republicans not falling too far behind Democrats in terms of turnout and enthusiasm.”
The Republican Party of Florida filed suit last Friday against the Florida Democratic Party, many of its candidates and a slew of television stations, seeking to stop the airing of a political ad highlighting the leaked grand jury presentment in the Hope Florida scandal.
What topics drive voter preferences?
Florida voters were split depending on the issue.
Jolly leads Donalds on handling data centers (41% to 37%), while Donalds holds the advantage on property insurance (43% to 38%).
The two candidates remain deadlocked on affordability and cost of living, with Jolly at 43% and Donalds at 42%.
Both Republican candidates benefit from higher enthusiasm within their base.
Seventy-seven percent of Donalds’ supporters express strong backing compared to 67% for Jolly.
In the U.S.
Senate race, 79% of Moody’s voters support her strongly compared to 75% for Nixon.
“Both Donalds and Moody enjoy a small but real enthusiasm gap among their voters,” Dr.
Freeder said.
“This is perhaps understandable given that former Republican Jolly may be less appealing to Democratic voters further to the left, and leftist Nixon may alienate moderate Democrats with her positions on the economy and Israel.”
Amendment 3: 14% remain undecided
The survey also polled Amendment 3, a proposed homestead property tax exemption measure.
Fifty percent indicated a "yes" vote—10 points short of the 60% supermajority required for passage—while 30% plan to vote "no" and 14% remain undecided.
The survey was conducted October 12–19, 2026, via telephone using a random sample of 1,471 likely midterm election voters.
The overall margin of sampling error is +/- 2.81 percentage points.

U.S.
Sen.
Ashley Moody leads Democrat Angie Nixon 49% to 45% in a new St.
Pete Polls survey for Florida Politics, her widest lead in three surveys by the pollster.
The sample is weighted 12 points Republican.
Ballots cast through Tuesday morning run Republican by less than one.
Another 3% picked someone else and 4% are undecided.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.
Republicans outnumber Democrats on the rolls by roughly 1.5 million, 5.69 million to 4.15 million at the Oct.
5 book closing, with 3.35 million more registered to no party.
The rolls are R+8.
The sample is R+12.
St.
Pete Polls’ mid-September survey had the race tied at 45%.
Its Oct.
5-7 survey had Moody ahead 47% to 45%.
Undecided voters have gone from 7% to 6% to 4%.
Nixon leads 56% to 41% among respondents who have already voted.
Moody leads 57% to 34% among those who have not.
Three in five Republican respondents said they had not voted yet.
Fewer than half of Democrats said the same.
Through Tuesday morning, Republicans had cast 40% of the 3.15 million ballots returned statewide and Democrats 39%, per the Division of Elections.
Voters outside the two parties cast the other 21%.
Democrats also hold more of the mail ballots still in circulation, 403,076 to 324,499.
In 2022, Republicans had out-voted Democrats by about 177,000 ballots at the same point in the calendar.
Reweighted to R+10, the same responses give Moody 48% to 45%.
At the registration split, it is 47% to 46%.
Nixon leads independents 53% to 36%, up from 49% to 36% in the October survey and 50% to 37% in September.
Moody holds 84% of Republicans, up from 82%.
Nixon holds 83% of Democrats, unchanged.
Men back Moody 50% to 43% after favoring Nixon 48% to 45% in October.
Women back Moody 49% to 45%.
Voters 70 and older back Moody 66% to 29%.
Nixon leads voters under 30 by 64% to 28%, those 30 to 49 by 52% to 39%, and those 50 to 69 by 48% to 46%.
White voters favor Moody 59% to 35%.
Black voters favor Nixon 77% to 17%, and Hispanic voters favor her 51% to 41%.
Moody leads the Tampa market 51% to 42%, Jacksonville 52% to 39%, Orlando 50% to 44%, West Palm Beach 48% to 46%, and Fort Myers 62% to 33%.
Nixon leads Miami 49% to 46%.
The University of North Florida’s survey released last week had the same numbers, Moody 49% to 45%.
St.
Pete Polls surveyed 916 likely voters Oct.
25-27 for Florida Politics, using automated phone calls for 71% of responses and peer-to-peer text messages for 29%.
Respondents were drawn at random from the state’s registered voter file as of Oct.
14.
Results were weighted by political party, race, age, gender, and media market to match Florida’s active voter population.
The weighted sample is 43% Republican, 31% Democratic, and 27% other.
Voters who said they do not plan to vote in the General Election were excluded.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.
—

The designee must submit an affidavit to pick-up the voter’s blank ballot.
Form DS-DE 162 is a combination form that includes the affidavit for ballot pick-up, the written authorization for the designee and if a request is not already on record, the voter’s request for a vote-by-mail ballot.
If a voter or designee waits until the start of mandatory early voting or up through Election Day to pick up or have delivered a vote-by-mail ballot, a special affidavit must also be completed.
The voter must affirm in the affidavit that an emergency exists that keeps the voter from being able to vote at a designated early voting site in his or her county or at his or her assigned polling place on Election Day.
The affidavit is part of Form DS-DE 162.
How Do I Request Another Ballot?
If a ballot is lost or damaged (e.g., not yet arrived or way overdue, return envelope has sealed due to humidity, ballot materials are wet, stained from food, torn, etc.), a voter can request another ballot.
Contact your Supervisor of Elections' office.
Contact information is here.
What is the Deadline to Return a Vote-by-Mail Ballot?
A returned voted ballot must be received, regardless of postmark, by the Supervisor of Elections' office no later than 7:00 pm (local time) on Election Day.
A 10-day extension exists for overseas voters only for Presidential Preference Primary and General Elections, provided the ballot is postmarked or dated by Election Day.
Untimely received ballots are otherwise not counted.
What is the Recommended Timeline to Return a Vote-by-Mail Ballot?
The United States Postal Service recommends that domestic nonmilitary voters mail back their voted ballots at least one (1) week before the Election Day deadline to account for any unforeseen events or weather issues.
The Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) provides recommended earlier timelines (see timetable at the bottom of FVAP's website) for absent military and overseas voters.
For more information about election mail and the United States Postal Service, visit the webpage on election-mail.
Where Do I Return a Vote-by-Mail Ballot?
A vote-by-mail ballot can be returned by mail or delivered in person.
If returned by mail, it can be returned by the United States Postal service or through another private or commercial carrier as long as the ballot is received by the requisite deadline.
A vote-by-mail ballot cannot be returned online, by fax, by email or by fax with one exception.
Overseas voters (civilian and military) have the option to return their ballot by mail or by fax.
Please visit the webpage Military and Overseas Voting for more information.

Safekeeping of mailed ballots; deadline for receiving vote-by-mail ballots.
101.67 Safekeeping of mailed ballots; deadline for receiving vote-by-mail ballots.—
(1)(a) The supervisor of elections shall safely keep in his or her office any envelopes received containing marked ballots of absent electors, and he or she shall, before the canvassing of the election returns, deliver the envelopes to the county canvassing board along with his or her file or list kept regarding said ballots.
(b) To the extent practicable, the supervisor of elections shall segregate any vote-by-mail ballots received from a person to whom notice has been sent pursuant to s.
98.075(7), but for whom a final determination of eligibility has not been made, and shall treat them as provisional ballots for individual review by the county canvassing board.
The supervisor shall attempt to contact each voter whose ballot has been set aside under this paragraph in the same manner as if the voter had voted a provisional ballot under s.
101.048.
(2) Except as provided in s.
101.6952(5), all marked absent electors’ ballots to be counted must be received by the supervisor by 7 p.m.
the day of the election.
All ballots received thereafter shall be marked with the time and date of receipt and filed in the supervisor’s office.

All eight men were charged together in a two-count indictment returned in Columbus today.
The indictment stems from an initial investigation and criminal complaint filed in the Southern District of Ohio against Tycen C.
Proper 19, of Danville, Ohio.
Proper and four others charged federally by criminal complaint in Missouri, Nebraska and California were arrested the weekend of the UFC event.
Two more defendants were charged by criminal complaint and arrested by the FBI approximately one week later in Washington and Missouri.
This week, an eighth defendant, Chandler D.
Scaggs, 21, of Chapmanville, West Virginia, was taken into custody in West Virginia.
Scaggs was allegedly assigned to be one of the snipers in the plotted attack.
An affidavit details that Scaggs was to be picked up by Proper to travel to Washington, D.C.
Scaggs and others lost contact with Proper upon Proper’s arrest, but Scaggs allegedly indicated to the group that he was still willing to participate in the attack and made new plans for another coconspirator to pick him up to travel to the UFC Freedom 250 event.

Washington — The FBI said Tuesday that it disrupted an attempt to attack Sunday's UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House.
Court records detail an alleged plot to use small drones carrying explosives and snipers to target senior government officials and wealthy attendees.
Five people have been charged for their alleged roles in the scheme: Tycen Proper of Ohio, Daniel Eskridge of Missouri, Abraham Hermosillo Alvarez of Nebraska, and Bryan Omar Roa and Michael Alan Thomas of California.
Each has been arrested and is being detained pending additional proceedings.
Affidavits filed across the four criminal cases detailed the alleged plot to target the UFC event at the White House on Sunday, with varying levels of involvement from the five defendants.
The filings detail numerous grievances against the government and federal officials, including U.S.
support for Israel, the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files and data centers.
The White House hosted the UFC fight series on Sunday — President Trump's 80th birthday — as part of the celebrations of the nation's 250th anniversary.
Thousands turned out to watch the fights on the White House South Lawn, where Mr.
Trump sat in the front row.
The potential targets laid out in the court filings included President Trump, Vice President JD Vance, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Elon Musk.
A number of elected officials were also named, including Tennessee Sen.
Marsha Blackburn, Arkansas Sen.
Tom Cotton and members of West Virginia's congressional delegation.
The defendants have each been charged with at least one count of conspiracy to commit murder.
Proper, 19, faces three additional charges, according to court filings.
Two law enforcement sources told CBS News that officials seized weapons, thousands of rounds of ammunition and tactical gear from the suspects during the execution of search warrants.
Sources said that no drones have actually been recovered.
Use of the drones was believed to be in the discussion-and-research phases, the sources said.
Federal investigators became aware of the alleged plot based on a tip from Proper's mother, who was concerned about his recent behavior, according to an affidavit submitted by an FBI agent in his case.

FBI Director Kash Patel revealed the existence of the alleged plot earlier Tuesday.
"On June 10, FBI and our law enforcement partners became aware of a potential threat to the UFC America 250 event in Washington, D.C.
involving individuals outside of the National Capital Region — and thanks to the rapid action of this FBI, our partners, and the Department of Justice in a multi-state operation, multiple individuals are now in custody and allegedly planned attacks were stopped cold," Patel wrote in a post on X.

Quinn added, "The event itself, I am confident in saying, was never at risk due to the great investigative work."

| MADISON — Gov.
Tony Evers announced today that the Wisconsin National Guard will assist local election officials as poll workers for the November 3 election across Wisconsin.

The troops will be released from duty Wednesday, November 4.

Attorney General Brian L.
Schwalb today issued a know-your-rights advisory on poll monitoring and voter intimidation for District residents.
DC and federal law protect the rights of District residents and all Americans to vote in a free and fair election without intimidation, coercion, or outside interference.
“Voting in DC is simple, secure, and reliable,” said Attorney General Schwalb.
“Anyone who experiences or witnesses interference with our local elections should report potential violations to our office and the DC Board of Elections.”
Voter Advisory: Protecting DC Residents from Unauthorized Poll Monitoring and Voter Intimidation
For guidance on your rights as a District of Columbia voter, read the FAQs provided below.
Can federal officials send the military, National Guard, and/or federal law enforcement to monitor the polls?
No.
An array of federal statutes bars federal employees, law enforcement, and the military from using their official power to interfere with an election.
Federal law generally prohibits the federal government from sending the military or “armed men,” including federal law-enforcement officers or National Guard troops, to a polling place.
Federal law also forbids anyone from intimidating or coercing voters in federal elections and from interfering with an election officer’s discharge of their duties.
National Guard troops deployed in the District have been specifically directed not to monitor or secure polling locations.
And federal law bars federal and local officials from using their authority to interfere with or affect a presidential or congressional election—such as using their official authority to help a particular candidate or party.
Can federal officials use the military to interfere with the election?
No.
Federal law prohibits the armed forces from denying the right to vote, interfering in an election, or preventing election administrators from performing their duties.
Can federal officials send armed ICE agents to polls?
No.
Federal law generally bars the federal government from sending armed persons to election locations.
Any armed federal agents—whether with ICE, the FBI, the U.S.
Marshals, or any other agency—cannot be sent to polling places.
Can federal officials order local law-enforcement officials to monitor the polls?
No.
Authority over federal law enforcement generally does not extend to local law enforcement.
In addition, as with federal actors, DC government employees can face criminal sanctions if they interfere with a presidential or congressional elect
[...]
 any vote counter while that person is counting ballots, or obstruct the election process.
As discussed in the previous paragraph, election monitors from the Department of Justice must follow all these rules, too.
Know Your Rights
If someone interferes with your right to vote through threats, intimidation, or coercion, or if you become aware of any interference with the right of DC residents to vote, please contact OAG at (202) 727-3400 or email us at OAGVoting@dc.gov, or contact BOE at 202-727-2194 or ogc@dcboe.org.
Voting in the District of Columbia
District residents can find information about the November elections, registering to vote, and voting by mail or in person on the DC Board of Elections website: www.dcboe.org.
In the District, all registered voters will be mailed a ballot.
Voters can return their mail-in ballot by mail using the enclosed prepaid envelope.
Mail ballots must be postmarked by Election Day (Tuesday, November 3, 2026) and must arrive no later than November 13.
If you plan to mail in your ballot, the Board of Elections recommends doing so as early as possible.
The signature on your mail-in ballot must match a signature on file with the Board of Elections.
Voters can also drop off their ballot at one of dozens of mail-ballot drop-box locations before 8:00 p.m.
on Election Day or at one of the vote centers during early voting (Monday, October 26, 2026–Sunday, November 1, 2026) or on Election Day.
You can track the status of your mail-in ballot online.
Mail-in ballots began arriving during the first week of October, but if voters do not receive a ballot by October 30, officials recommend planning to vote in person.
If voters don’t plan to vote by mail, they can find convenient early vote centers and Election Day vote centers online, which will be open every day from 8:30 a.m.
to 7:00 p.m.
during early voting and from 7:00 a.m.
to 8:00 p.m.
on Election Day.
Voters can vote at any of the vote centers during early voting and on Election Day.
Unregistered voters can also register in person during early voting or on Election Day itself.
More information on registering to vote is here.

"Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material," Caine added.

The Pentagon told Military.com it had nothing more to add beyond the content of the letter.

Slotkin's letter grew out of a broader unease among Democrats about the administration's willingness to domestically use the military.
She told the AP that President Donald Trump has been laying the groundwork to claim the elections were stolen by the opposition party.
Caine, the nation's highest-ranking military officer, said that no such plan or agenda exists.

This is a civilian function it has carried out in past elections.

The Posse Comitatus Act restricts the use of federal troops for domestic law enforcement.
Legal analysts note it does not apply to National Guard members operating under state command.
A separate federal law bars troops at polling places except to repel armed enemies of the country.
The main exception to these limits is the Insurrection Act, which a president can invoke to use the military domestically in certain circumstances.
Caine has ruled out the federal military carrying out such actions on its own.

National Guard, DOJ monitors headed to some Washington counties ahead of Election Day
WASHINGTON STATE — With one week until Election Day, several Washington counties are getting help from the National Guard to keep ballot drop boxes secure.
The Department of Justice is also sending election monitors to some counties, including King County.
King, Pierce, Thurston, Clark and Snohomish counties have all accepted the governor’s offer of National Guard help.
The move follows past incidents, including a ballot drop box set on fire in Vancouver, Washington, in 2024, and letters containing white powder sent to election offices and officials, including the Washington secretary of state.
Election officials say Guard members will be unarmed, wear plain clothes, and only monitor drop boxes.
They will not handle ballots, interact with voters or act as law enforcement.
“These folks will supplement our existing security plans and just provide extra eyes and ears out there in the community,” said Halei Watkins with King County Elections.
RELATED | Gov.
Ferguson offers unarmed, out-of-uniform Guard observers to deter ballot box threats
In Pierce County, Auditor Linda Farmer says Guard teams will watch the drop boxes overnight and visit all 57 that are accessible.
“They’ll be observing and reporting and just making sure that nothing’s going on,” Farmer said.
Pierce County has taken other steps since receiving a similar suspicious letter in 2023.
A Pierce County sheriff’s deputy is now stationed at the elections center, and various drop boxes have cameras and fire suppression systems.
“In this line of work, we’re always planning for contingencies, but it used to be earthquakes and power outages and equipment failures,” Farmer said.
“Now it’s things that are a little bit more serious.”
“We have upgraded the glass in our observation corridor to be bullet-resistant, and so we’re doing several things seen and unseen to make sure that vote is protected,” Farmer added.
The DOJ monitors will also be in certain areas, including King County, to make sure election offices are complying with federal election law, including the Voting Rights Act, according to King County Elections officials.
“DOJ has always sent out monitors to keep an eye on elections to see if there’s anything they can do to improve the system or to answer questions, to help with cooperation,” said Neil Floyd, acting U.S.
attorney for the Western District of Washington.
DOJ officials added that they are only monitoring the election process and will not be checking individual voter eligibility.
Election officials say voters will likely not notice the Guard, since members will be in plain clothes and focused on drop boxes overnight.
The governor’s office says they could begin later this week.

Background
On June 10, 2024, the Commission published a notice of proposed
rulemaking in the Federal Register proposing amendments to its rules
concerning event contracts in certain excluded commodities.

types of event contracts that fall within the scope of section

contrary to the public interest, such that they may not be listed for
trading or accepted for clearing on or through a CFTC-registered
entity.

the types of event contracts that involve ``gaming.''

The Commission is withdrawing these proposed rules to reconsider
them in light of various forms of state regulatory actions and
litigation concerning the Commission's exclusive jurisdiction over
event contract derivatives listed on designated contract markets and
the proper application of the swap and excluded commodity definitions
under the Commodity Exchange Act, including issues related to the
preemption of state gambling, wagering, and gaming laws in relation to
sports-related event contracts laws and what activities constitute
``gaming'' under the CEA.\2\ Thus, the Commission no longer intends to
issue final rules with respect to the proposal.

For example, as of September 1, 2026, at least seven DCMs registered with the CFTC offer contracts that include event contracts based on sports-related events to U.S.

In August 2026, average monthly trading volume in event contracts was about $1.5 billion across all DCMs reporting to the Commission.[127] Of that volume, approximately $1.2 billion was in event contracts based on sports-related events; approximately $11 million was in event contracts based on politics-related events, including elections-related event contracts; and approximately $4 million was in event contracts based on weather-related events.[128]
Because the Commission does not expect the Proposal to change the legal rights or obligations of market participants under the CEA, it is the Commission's preliminary belief that the primary benefit of this Proposal would be added certainty that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps that are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the CFTC.
Although the extent of the benefit may be limited by the ongoing efforts of certain state regulators to assert their jurisdiction over certain event contracts, market participants—including DCMs listing event contracts— may benefit by spending less time and fewer resources determining which regulatory regime applies and by saving the costs of complying with various State regulatory regimes.
It is the Commission's preliminary belief that there should be negligible costs from codifying that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps subject to the Commission's exclusive jurisdiction, as there would be no expected changes required of market participants under the CEA or the Commission's regulations.

For the purpose of this section:
(1) Exemptive letter means a written grant of relief issued by the staff of a Division of the Commission from the applicability of a specific provision of the Act or of a rule, regulation or order issued thereunder by the Commission.
An exemptive letter may only be issued by staff of a Division when the Commission itself has exemptive authority and that authority has been delegated by the Commission to the Division in question.
An exemptive letter binds the Commission and its staff with respect to the relief provided therein.
Only the Beneficiary may rely upon the exemptive letter.

(1) Issuance of a Letter is entirely within the discretion of Commission staff.

Commission staff may reject or decline to respond to a request that does not comply with the requirements of this section.

ntributions to the congressman’s campaign, all between $10 and $20.
In both cases, the gifts appear to have been made via the digital fundraising platform ActBlue.
For the most part, Jones hasn’t been able to gain traction with that sort of low-profile donor.
Nor does he court powerful PACs like the American Bankers Association (which gave Thompson $10,000 this quarter), Comcast Corporation & NBCUNIVERSAL ($7,500) or The Home Depot ($10,000), among dozens of others.
Thompson, unlike Jones, also remains aligned with prominent civic and business figures, especially in Napa and Sonoma counties, which remain part of the 4th District after Prop 50 gerrymandering.
The congressman’s donors in the third quarter included three of five Napa County supervisors, Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, former U.S.
Rep.
Barbara Boxer and California Treasurer Fiona Ma, who is running for lieutenant governor.
Notable wine families such as the Mondavis, Beckstoffers and Cakebreads have kicked in, as have both the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria and their chairman, Greg Sarris.
Evident in the updated figures: Jones’ fundraising is slowing down, despite heavy advertising buys.
His total contributions for the quarter, minus his own spending, was $176,800.
Previously this year, he’d received about $3 million.
Thompson’s gifts have waned as well, but not as steeply.
He pulled in around $1 million in the third quarter — $518,000 from individuals and $484,000 from PACS.
For the election cycle, he’s at just over $5 million.
Jones far outspent his incumbent rival in the quarter, shelling out $4.3 million to Thompson’s $560,000.
The campaign went $3.7 million in debt to help get the challenger there.
For the cycle, the gap in total expenditures is $11.8 million by Jones to $4.9 million by Thompson.
Only five California political campaigns have ever self-financed more heavily than Jones in an electoral cycle, according to the CalMatters data.
They include the gubernatorial runs of Tom Steyer, Meg Whitman, Steve Westly and Steve Poizner, and Poizner’s bid for insurance commissioner.
The news outlet didn’t include presidential campaigns.
Perhaps the most relevant number of all, at least to the two 4th District campaigns, is cash on hand.
As of Sept.
30, Thompson had about $1.5 million to work with, while Jones had just under $1.2 million.
That’s on the high end for a race entering the stretch run.
What does it mean for constituents?
In all likelihood, another flurry of mailers, TV ads and new yard signs over the remaining two weeks of the campaign.

This analysis is among all registered voters – many of whom will not turn out in this November’s midterm elections.
For example, 46% of those eligible voted in the 2022 midterm elections.
While those who turn out in elections often differ from those who do not, including in their vote choice, the ways groups of voters overall view the choice illustrate wide – and familiar – differences in voting preferences by gender, race, education, age and political party.
Gender
Men are evenly divided: 42% say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their district, and 42% say they would vote for the Republican.
Women support Democratic candidates by a 14-point margin, 45% vs.
31% for Republicans.
Race and ethnicity
White voters tilt toward Republicans, 44% to 37%.
Among Hispanic voters, Democratic candidates hold a 51% to 24% advantage.
A quarter of Hispanic voters say they would support another candidate or are not sure.
In the 2024 presidential election, Hispanic voters were nearly evenly split in their vote preference.
But in previous midterm and presidential elections over the past two decades, they have supported Democrats by considerable margins.
Seven-in-ten Black voters support Democratic candidates, while 7% back Republicans.
Among Asian voters, 56% support Democrats, and 16% choose Republicans.
A combined 27% would vote for another candidate or are not sure.
Age
As in previous midterm elections, younger voters tilt Democratic.
Voters ages 50 and older are more divided:
- Voters ages 18 to 29 prefer Democrats over Republicans by a two-to-one margin: 51% to 23%.
A quarter say they are not sure or would support another candidate.
- Voters 30 to 49 tilt toward Democrats – 43% vs.

Midterm preferences and engagement
Voters who are highly attentive to this year’s elections favor Democrats by a wide margin.

The Democratic advantage is not as wide among all those who turned out to vote in either the most recent presidential (2024) or midterm (2022) elections.
Vote preference among highly engaged voters
- Among voters who say they have given a lot of thought to the election, Democrats lead Republicans, 58% to 34%.
- Among voters who say it really matters who wins, Democrats lead, 53% to 38%.
- Among voters who say they are extremely motivated to vote, Democrats lead, 59% to 35%.
Democrats’ leads contrast the last midterm elections in 2022, when voters who said it really mattered who won or were extremely motivated were evenly divided in their preferences, and those who had given a lot of thought tilted to GOP candidates.
Vote preference and turnout in recent elections
Compared with Democrats’ wide advantages among the most engaged voters, Democrats hold more modest leads among voters who have a validated record of voting in the 2024 presidential election (45% to 39%) and those who voted in both 2024 and 2022 (47% to 41%).
Democrats also lead among voters who didn’t vote in 2024 or 2022.
However, roughly one-in-three of these 2024 or 2022 nonvoters say they support a third-party candidate or are not sure – a larger share than those who voted in 2024 (16%) or 2022 (13%).

polymarket-4927096.text:
Democrats’ 49% to 39% advantage among registered voters nationally is the largest in CNN polling since just before the 2020 election, and rests on wide margins among traditional pillars of Democratic support such as Black voters (who favor the Democrats by 70 percentage points), Latino voters (+40), women (+21) and younger adults (+31), as well as a steep advantage among independents (+15) and those who say they’re extremely motivated to vote (+18).
Trump’s support has also eroded among White Americans without college degrees, a group that has formed a core part of the president’s Republican base.
Trump’s approval is underwater among the group: 45% approve, down from 63% at the start of his second term.
The CNN poll was conducted by SSRS from October 15-18 among a random national sample of 1,701 US adults drawn from a probability-based panel, including 1,206 registered voters.

The Democratic Party, riding a tide of anti-Donald Trump sentiment, enters the final stretch of the midterm campaign with a 10-point advantage over Republicans nationwide in voters’ choice in their own congressional district, according to a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS.
More than three-quarters of voters see this election as their chance to change things up in Washington, the poll finds.
Trump’s approval rating stands at a record low of 32%, and voters express broad dissatisfaction with both the economy and the state of the country nearly two years into unified GOP control of the federal government.
Those sentiments work against the GOP in its effort to hold on to Congress, even as some voters express skepticism that a Democratic win would bring meaningful improvement.
Democrats’ 49% to 39% advantage among registered voters nationally is the largest in CNN polling since just before the 2020 election, and rests on wide margins among traditional pillars of Democratic support such as Black voters (who favor the Democrats by 70 percentage points), Latino voters (+40), women (+21) and younger adults (+31), as well as a steep advantage among independents (+15) and those who say they’re extremely motivated to vote (+18).
Even with those broad advantages, the scale of the Democratic Party’s potential gains could be limited by mid-decade redistricting and the large number of competitive races in GOP-friendly territory.
Should a 10-point margin in favor of the Democrats materialize in the nationwide popular vote, that would represent roughly a 13-point swing from the nationwide popular vote for House in 2024.
But even a swing that large may not ultimately translate into deep-red pickups for the party, as many of this year’s competitive campaigns are playing out in places that Trump carried by double digits.
The Democratic upper-hand has held over the past year, and the margin has widened in recent polling as cost-of-living concerns remain voters’ most important i
[...]
 in using his presidential power and overseeing deportations, nearly 7 in 10 say he has not gone far enough in trying to reduce prices.
Erosion in Trump’s base
Democratic opposition to Trump, of course, was potent even in the brighter environment of 2018.
But the survey suggests it’s the collapse in economic sentiment that’s further eroded Trump’s base throughout his second term in office, leaving him in his most precarious position to date.
Trump’s approval rating among Republicans hits a new numeric low in the poll at 74%, down from 88% in February 2025.
Younger Republicans and Republican-leaning independents are particularly sour on Trump’s presidency and the state of the country.
Nearly 4 in 10 Republican-aligned adults younger than 45 disapprove of Trump.
They also rate Trump roughly 20 points worse than older Republicans on the economy, inflation and the way he sets priorities.
Although younger voters are generally less motivated to vote than older ones, the gap is particularly large on the Republican side: There’s a 29-point gap in strong motivation to vote between younger and older Republican-aligned adults, compared with a 15-point gap on the Democratic side.
Trump’s support has also eroded among White Americans without college degrees, a group that has formed a core part of the president’s Republican base.
Trump’s approval is underwater among the group: 45% approve, down from 63% at the start of his second term.
And strong disapproval is now almost double strong approval among this group (40% to 22%).
That negativity appears tied to economic concerns.
While a majority of White adults without degrees still approve of Trump’s handling of immigration (53%) and voting rights and election integrity (55%), 64% now disapprove of his handling of the economy and 68% disapprove on inflation.
Voters aren’t completely sold on Democrats either
Amid all the negativity about Trump, though, a sizable share of voters say they don’t think the country would be better off if Democrats won control of Congress either.
In the new poll, 41% of voters say the country would be better off should Democrats win in November, 37% that it would be worse off and 22% say it wouldn’t make any difference.
The sense that a change in power in Congress wouldn’t move the needle for the country is notably high among independent voters (36% feel that way), Latino voters (29%) and political moderates (29%).
Both parties continue to have net negative favorability ratings.
The 18% of voters who hold negative views of both parties break 48% for the Democrat in their district to 28% for the Republican, with 18% saying they don’t support either party’s candidate.
This group overwhelmingly says their votes are about changing things in Washington (90%) but largely sees neither party as able to do a better job of bringing it (65%).
Roughly half of registered voters in the poll say they plan to vote on Election Day, with the rest planning to vote early or by mail; about 13% overall say they have already cast their ballot.
Those who’ve already voted break overwhelmingly for Democrats – 70% to 29%.
Those who have yet to cast a ballot and will be the focus of the final days of campaigning are much more closely divided: 46% favor the Democrat in their district to 41% who favor the Republican.
CNN’s Isabelle LaBianco and Katie Doran contributed to this report.
The CNN poll was conducted by SSRS from October 15-18 among a random national sample of 1,701 US adults drawn from a probability-based panel, including 1,206 registered voters.
Surveys were either conducted online or by telephone with a live interviewer.
Results for the full sample have a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points; it is 3.3 points among registered voters.

Democrats Hold Clear Lead in Our Final Generic Congressional Ballot Poll
How the race has moved (9 polls)
ActiVote’s October 30, 2026 Generic Congressional Ballot poll, our final poll of this race before the midterm elections, finds that the Democrats lead the Republicans by 7.0%.
The poll was in the field between October 22 and October 30 (median field date of October 26).
For this final reading we doubled our usual sample: the poll was among 2000 likely midterm voters and has an average expected error of 2.2%.
The Republicans lead among rural voters, men, voters 50 and older, registered Republicans, White voters and the (moderate) right.
Voters with a high school education are evenly split.
Democrats lead among all other groups, including suburban and urban voters, voters under 50, women, independents, Black and Latino voters, voters on low, middle and high incomes, and college-educated voters and graduate degree holders.
These group figures rest on subsamples for which the expected error is considerably larger than the 2.2% for the poll as a whole.
Compared with our October 21 poll, the Democratic lead narrowed slightly, from 7.4% to 7.0%.
Political Spectrum
The following graph shows the support for Democrats and Republicans among left, moderate left, center, moderate right, and right voters.
These groups are defined by splitting the national electorate in 5 equal sized groups of 20% each
The left (99%) and the moderate left (97%) are virtually unanimous in their support for the Democrats, as is the right (98%) in its support for the Republicans.
The moderate right is 85% Republican.
Among centrists the Democrats lead by 54% to 46%.

The “generic ballot” is a type of survey question that asks voters to choose which party they prefer in the US House of Representatives.
Taken as a whole, generic ballot polling provides a broad look at where the parties stand nationwide ahead of a congressional election.
This CNN Poll of Polls average includes the most recent non-partisan national surveys that meet CNN’s standards and ask registered or likely voters which party’s congressional candidate they would support in their own district.

Democrats with 8-Point Advantage Heading Into Midterm Elections...
Plurality Says Vote is Mainly Against the President
A majority of likely voters nationally say they are more likely to vote for the Democratic running for Congress in their district rather than the Republican, giving the Democrats an 8-point lead on the generic congressional ballot question.
With negative views toward President Donald Trump permeating the electoral landscape, a plurality of likely voters say their congressional vote is one in opposition to the president.
- The Democratic candidates running for Congress (52%) lead the Republican candidates (44%) among likely voters nationally.
Among registered voters, the Democrats have a 10-point lead.
In September, the Democrats had a 12-point advantage on the generic congressional ballot question among registered voters.
- Democratic congressional candidates (52%) have a double-digit lead against the Republicans (39%) among independents who are likely to vote.
- A majority of likely voters (51%) think the Democrat running for Congress in their district will win compared with 46% who say the Republican will be elected.
- 44% of likely voters say their vote for Congress is mainly a vote against President Trump.
21% say their ballot is mainly in favor of the president while 35% say the president is not influencing their vote very much.
Independents are more than three times as likely to say their vote is mainly against President Trump (44%) than one in favor of him (12%).
- 55% of likely voters say it is more important to vote for candidates who will bring about change rather than to support candidates with experience and a proven track record (41%).

 healthcare (5%), crime (4%), abortion (2%), education (2%), and climate change (1%).
Nearly Four in Ten Say Family Finances Have Deteriorated
While 44% of likely voters say their personal finances have stayed about the same in the last year, 38% say that their personal finances have gotten worse.
15% say their financial picture has gotten better.
Democrats (51%) are more than twice as likely than Republicans (21%) to say their family finances have gotten worse.
Among registered voters nationally, more registered voters now say their finances have deteriorated (40% from 34% in September).
Those who say their finances have improved have inched down to 16% from 20%, previously.
Majority Perceives Negative Impact of Data Centers
Fueled by Democrats and independents, 59% of likely voters think the data centers being built around the country by tech companies have a negative impact on the country.
33% say they have a positive impact, and two percent are usure.
Opposition to data centers grows when likely voters consider their own communities.
66% of likely voters either oppose or strongly oppose these centers.
27% strongly favor or favor data centers being built in their communities.
Methodology
This NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll national survey of 1,289 registered voters was conducted October 19th through October 20th, 2026, by the Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News.
Registered voters 18 years of age and older residing in the United States were contacted through a multi-mode design: By phone using live interviewers, by text, or online.
Results for registered voters are statistically significant within ±3.7 percentage points.
Results for likely voters are statistically significant within ±3.8 percentage points.

Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services.
The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S.
population.
It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers.
Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals.
Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U).
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months.
The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living.
Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments).
All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index.
Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations.
Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas.
Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.

Background
About Inflation Nowcasting
The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland provides daily “nowcasts” of inflation for two popular price indexes, the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE) and the consumer price index (CPI).
Nowcasts are estimates or forecasts of the present.
The Cleveland Fed produces nowcasts of the current period's rate of inflation—inflation in a given month or quarter—before the official CPI or PCE inflation data are released.
These forecasts can help to give a sense of where inflation is now and where it is likely to be in the future.
Our inflation nowcasts are produced with a model that uses a small number of available data series at different frequencies, including daily oil prices, weekly gasoline prices, and monthly CPI and PCE inflation readings.
The model generates nowcasts of monthly inflation, and these are combined for nowcasting current-quarter inflation.
As with any forecast, there is no guarantee that these inflation nowcasts will be accurate all of the time.
But historically, the Cleveland Fed’s model nowcasts have done quite well—in many cases, they have been more accurate than common benchmarks from alternative statistical models and even consensus inflation nowcasts from surveys of professional forecasters.
Revisions and special notices
The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release an October 2025 CPI report due to the suspension of federal government services.
See this document for a detailed description of how the inflation nowcasting indicator handled the November 2025 CPI report.

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:
The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.
While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated.
The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
The Committee will deliver price stability.
Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D.
Cook and Beth M.
Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

contain month-over-month inflation rates for October and November 2025 for most series,
including CPI and core CPI, which are inputs into the inflation nowcasting model.
To generate month-over-month inflation rates for October 2025 to be used in nowcasting future
months, we used the inflation nowcasting model’s estimates available as of December 17, 2025,
for monthly CPI and core CPI inflation, along with the other series that enter the model.
We used
those month-over-month estimates to produce estimated price levels for the series for October
2025, and we assume that the year-over-year inflation rates for those series will be unchanged
going forward, which is relevant for series subject to seasonal adjustment.
Based on those
estimated price levels for October 2025 and the price levels for November 2025 produced by the
BLS, we then calculate the implied month-over-month inflation readings for November 2025.
The
October and November 2025 month-over-month CPI and core CPI estimates are thus model-
dependent and not official monthly inflation readings from the BLS.

Currently, the
reference base for most CPI indexes is 1982-

The reference base years
refer to the period in which the index is set to
100.0.
In addition, expenditure weights are
updated every two years to keep the CPI

Index numbers are not dollar values, but
measures of the change over time relative to
their base period value of 100.0 (for example,
280.0 or 30.3).
Index numbers also are
commonly used to measure the size and
direction of price movements between various
time periods such as monthly, quarterly, semi-
annual, and annual percent changes.
Effective with the January 2007 CPI, the
Bureau of Labor Statistics began to publish its
consumer price indexes rounded to three
decimal places rather than one.
As a result,
all percent changes in this document have
been calculated from three decimal place
indexes regardless of date.
However, the
resulting percent changes will continue to be
published to one decimal place.
Note: using
three decimal place values to compute percent
changes eliminates nearly all rounding errors
in the resulting percent change that
occasionally occurred when using indexes
rounded to one decimal place.
Additional
information on this conversion can be found
at www.bls.gov/cpi/cpithreedec.htm.
What follows are mathematical concepts and
formulae that are useful in a variety of index
applications.
Percent change
Movements of an index from one month to
another are usually expressed as percent
changes rather than as changes in index
points, because index point changes are
affected by the level of the index in relation to
its base period, while percent changes are not.
The following illustration shows a
hypothetical CPI one-month change between
April 2016 and May 2016 using the 1982-
84=100 reference base.
Reference Base
1982-84=100
May 2016 ........................................
240.236
April 2016 .......................................
239.261
Index point change ..............................
0.975
Divided by the earlier index .....
0.975/239.261
Equals ...............................................
0.004075
Multiplied by 100 ...............................
0.4075
Equals percent change ........................
0.4

T o a r r i v e a t a p e r c e n t c h a n g e o v e r a n e n t i r e
year, the beginning and ending periods of a
CPI series must always be the same month,
such as May 2015 and May 2016.
Note: A
calculation using January and December data
would result in an 11-month change, not a 12-
month/over-the-year change.
The calculation below shows the over-the-
year change from May 2015 to May 2016 for
both the 1982-84=100 and 1967=100
reference bases.
The percent change is
rounded:
Reference Base
1982-84=100 1967=100
May 2015 237.805 712.357
May 2016 240.236 719.641
Index point change 2.431 7.284
Divided by the
earlier index 2.431/237.805 7.284/712.357
Equals 0.01022 0.01022
Multiplied by 100 1.022 1.022
Equals percent change 1.0 1.0

1.
Always use the same reference base period
for all calculations.
If the first point uses the
1982-84=100 base, the end point must also
use that base.

2.
Calculating an over-the-year percent
change, such as May 2015 to May 2016, is not
equal to the sum of the over-the-month
changes between those two time periods.
Annual averages
Annual averages are the sum of the 12
monthly data points (i.e .
indexes), divided by
12.
They represent an average index for a
given year, not a particular month.
An annual
average change should not be confused with
the over the year percent change, such as the
calculation of the May to May changes
mentioned above.
A percent change from December 2014 to
December 2015 is unlikely to be the same as
the change in the annual average from 2014 to
2015.
Users should take care to examine the
data with which the CPI is being compared to
determine whether the annual average or 12-
month change is more appropriate for their
purposes.

The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.6 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in
September after rising 0.4 percent in August, the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today.
Over the last 12
months, the all items index increased 3.7 percent before seasonal adjustment.
The index for gasoline rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase.
The
energy index increased 5.2 percent over the month following a 2.1-percent increase in August.
The shelter index rose 0.4
percent in September after rising 0.3 percent in August.
The index for food was unchanged in September, as the index for
food away from home increased 0.2 percent and the index for food at home fell 0.1 percent.
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in September, as it did in August.
Indexes that increased
over the month include recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care, and apparel.
Conversely,
the index for communication was among the small number of major indexes that decreased in September.
The all items index rose 3.7 percent for the 12 months ending September, a larger increase than the 3.4-percent increase
reported for the 12 months ending in August.
The all items less food and energy index rose 2.6 percent over the year,
following a 2.4-percent increase over the 12 months ending August.
The energy index increased 20.4 percent for the 12
months ending September.
The food index increased 2.5 percent over the last year.

Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services.
The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S.
population.
It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers.
Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals.
Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for

October 28, 2026
Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
For release at 2:00 p.m.
EDT
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:
The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.
While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated.
The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
The Committee will deliver price stability.
Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D.
Cook and Beth M.
Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.
For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955.

However, the resulting percent changes will continue to be published to one decimal place.

Currently, the
reference base for most CPI indexes is 1982-
84=100 but some indexes have other
references bases.
The reference base years
refer to the period in which the index is set to
100.0.
In addition, expenditure weights are
updated every two years to keep the CPI
current with changing consumer preferences.
Index numbers are not dollar values, but
measures of the change over time relative to
their base period value of 100.0 (for example,
280.0 or 30.3).
Index numbers also are
commonly used to measure the size and
direction of price movements between various
time periods such as monthly, quarterly, semi-
annual, and annual percent changes.
Effective with the January 2007 CPI, the
Bureau of Labor Statistics began to publish its
consumer price indexes rounded to three
decimal places rather than one.
As a result,
all percent changes in this document have
been calculated from three decimal place
indexes regardless of date.
However, the
resulting percent changes will continue to be
published to one decimal place.
Note: using
three decimal place values to compute percent
changes eliminates nearly all rounding errors
in the resulting percent change that
occasionally occurred when using indexes
rounded to one decimal place.
Additional
information on this conversion can be found
at www.bls.gov/cpi/cpithreedec.htm.
What follows are mathematical concepts and
formulae that are useful in a variety of index
applications.
Percent change
Movements of an index from one month to
another are usually expressed as percent
changes rather than as changes in index
points, because index point changes are
affected by the level of the index in relation to
its base period, while percent changes are not.

polymarket-5734062.text:
Updated: November 9, 2025 14:11 Xinhua
China's consumer price index (CPI), a main gauge of inflation, was up 0.2 percent year on year in October 2025, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed Sunday.

BEIJING, Nov.
9 -- China's consumer price index (CPI), a main gauge of inflation, was up 0.2 percent year on year in October 2025, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed Sunday.
On a monthly basis, the CPI also rose 0.2 percent last month, according to this data.
The core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, increased by 1.2 percent year on year -- marking the sixth consecutive month of acceleration in growth pace.
NBS statistician Dong Lijuan attributed the consumer price increase last month to the continued effects of policies to expand domestic demand, coupled with the boosting impact of the National Day and Mid-Autumn Festival holiday period.
Sunday's data also revealed that the producer price index, which measures costs for goods at the factory gate -- went down 2.1 percent year on year in October.

9月份，居民消费价格指数（CPI）环比上涨0.2%，涨幅比上月回落0.2个百分点；同比上涨0.9%，涨幅比上月扩大0.1个百分点；扣除食品和能源价格的核心CPI同比上涨1.0%，涨幅与上月相同。
汽油价格上涨16.6%，涨幅扩大7.3个百分点，影响CPI同比上涨约0.47个百分点，带动能源价格涨幅由上月的4.1%扩大至本月的7.3%。
食品价格下降1.7%，降幅比上月扩大0.3个百分点，影响CPI同比下降约0.29个百分点。食品中，猪肉和鲜菜价格分别下降10.0%和8.1%，合计影响CPI同比下降约0.33个百分点。

2026年9月份CPI、PPI同比涨幅均扩大
——国家统计局城市司首席统计师董莉娟解读2026年9月份CPI和PPI数据
9月份，居民消费价格指数（CPI）环比上涨0.2%，涨幅比上月回落0.2个百分点；同比上涨0.9%，涨幅比上月扩大0.1个百分点；扣除食品和能源价格的核心CPI同比上涨1.0%，涨幅与上月相同。工业生产者出厂价格指数（PPI）环比上涨1.2%，涨幅比上月扩大0.8个百分点；同比上涨5.0%，涨幅比上月扩大1.2个百分点。
一、CPI环比涨幅回落，同比涨幅扩大
从环比看，全国CPI上涨0.2%，涨幅比上月回落0.2个百分点。其中，服务价格由上月上涨0.1%转为下降0.2%，对CPI环比的影响由上月上拉约0.04个百分点转为下拉约0.08个百分点。服务中，随着暑假结束，飞机票、宾馆住宿和旅行社收费价格分别下降8.7%、7.0%和6.0%，合计影响CPI环比下降约0.12个百分点；秋季开学，教育服务价格上涨0.4%，影响CPI环比上涨约0.03个百分点。工业消费品价格上涨0.7%，涨幅比上月回落0.1个百分点，影响CPI环比上涨约0.22个百分点。工业消费品中，受国际市场价格变动影响，国内汽油价格上涨4.9%，涨幅比上月回落2.3个百分点，黄金饰品价格由上月上涨7.6%转为下降2.1%，两项合计影响CPI环比上涨约0.14个百分点；受成本走高影响，移动电话机、计算机、数据存储设备和平板电脑价格分别上涨3.7%、2.0%、1.7%和1.5%，合计影响CPI环比上涨约0.04个百分点；秋装上市，带动服装价格上涨0.7%，影响CPI环比上涨约0.03个百分点。食品价格上涨0.4%，涨幅与上月相同，低于季节性水平0.8个百分点，影响CPI环比上涨约0.06个百分点。食品中，鲜菜、猪肉、鸡蛋和鲜果价格涨幅在0.5%—2.3%之间，合计影响CPI环比上涨约0.05个百分点；牛肉和羊肉价格持续上涨，本月分别上涨3.1%和1.4%，涨幅均有扩大，合计影响CPI环比上涨约0.04个百分点；休渔期结束，水产品供应充足，价格下降0.8%，影响CPI环比下降约0.02个百分点。
从同比看，全国CPI上涨0.9%，涨幅比上月扩大0.1个百分点。其中，汽油价格上涨16.6%，涨幅扩大7.3个百分点，影响CPI同比上涨约0.47个百分点，带动能源价格涨幅由上月的4.1%扩大至本月的7.3%。扣除能源的工业消费品价格上涨1.6%，涨幅回落0.2个百分点，影响CPI同比上涨约0.39个百分点。其中，黄金饰品价格上涨22.5%，涨幅回落11.1个百分点，影响CPI同比上涨约0.11个百分点；数据存储设备、平板电脑、计算机和移动电话机价格分别上涨46.7%、23.6%、21.8%和14.9%，涨幅均有扩大，合计影响CPI同比上涨约0.23个百分点。服务价格上涨0.8%，涨幅与上月相同，影响CPI同比上涨约0.40个百分点。服务中，出行服务价格上涨2.1%，涨幅扩大0.8个百分点；医疗服务价格上涨4.0%，涨幅与上月相同。食品价格下降1.7%，降幅比上月扩大0.3个百分点，影响CPI同比下降约0.29个百分点。食品中，猪肉和鲜菜价格分别下降10.0%和8.1%，合计影响CPI同比下降约0.33个百分点；粮食、食用油、奶类和鲜果价格降幅在0.6%—1.5%之间，合计影响CPI同比下降约0.07个百分点；鸡蛋价格上涨17.4%，涨幅回落1.1个百分点，影响CPI同比上涨约0.07个百分点；牛肉和羊肉价格分别上涨7.5%和6.4%，涨幅继续扩大，合计影响CPI同比上涨约0.08个百分点。
二、PPI环比和同比涨幅均扩大
从环比看，全国PPI上涨1.2%，涨幅比上月扩大0.8个百分点。本月PPI环比运行的主要特点：一是国际原油、有色金属价格上行带动国内相关行业价格上涨。石油开采、精炼石油产品制造、有机化学原料制造价格分别上涨14.5%、7.4%和5.4%，有色金属矿采选业、有色金属冶炼和压延加工业价格分别上涨1.6%和1.5%，5个行业合计影响PPI环比上涨约0.63个百分点。二是部分能源和原材料行业供需状况变化拉动价格上涨。受冬季供暖备煤需求增加、主产矿区供应阶段性偏紧、国际煤价上涨预期效应等因素影响，煤炭开采和洗选业、煤炭加工价格分别上涨9.5%和13.6%；钢材、水泥等建筑材料需求有所回升，加之原材料成本上涨，非金属矿物制品业价格在连降7个月后转为上涨0.3%，黑色金属冶炼和压延加工业价格上涨0.2%，4个行业合计影响PPI环比上涨约0.38个百分点。三是人工智能、算电协同等领域加快发展带动部分行业需求增加、价格上涨。电气机械和器材制造业、计算机通信和其他电子设备制造业价格均上涨0.4%，2个行业合计影响PPI环比上涨约0.07个百分点。
从同比看，全国PPI上涨5.0%，涨幅比上月扩大1.2个百分点。分主要行业看，价格上涨的行业中，煤炭开采和洗选业上涨35.3%，石油和天然气开采业、石油煤炭及其他燃料加工业、化学原料和化学制品制造业分别上涨24.5%、21.6%和12.1%，有色金属矿采选业、有色金属冶炼和压延加工业均上涨21.4%，电气机械和器材制造业上涨6.2%，计算机通信和其他电子设备制造业上涨5.8%，8个行业涨幅比上月均扩大，合计影响PPI同比上涨约5.42个百分点，上拉影响比上月增加1.12个百分点。价格下降的行业中，酒饮料和精制茶制造业下降5.3%，电力热力生产和供应业下降3.9%，医药制造业下降3.3%，非金属矿物制品业下降2.5%，汽车制造业下降2.0%，5个行业合计下拉PPI同比约0.66个百分点。

国家统计局服务业调查中心和中国物流与采购联合会发布的数据显示，10月份，高技术制造业和装备制造业采购经理指数（PMI）分别为51.3%和50.6%，继续高于临界点，相关行业企业生产经营保持扩张，新质生产力延续良好发展态势。

服务业商务活动指数为50.0%，位于临界点。从行业看，主要服务业门类商务活动指数均有回升，其中与“十一”假期出行消费相关的铁路运输、住宿、文化体育娱乐等行业商务活动指数回升明显，且均位于扩张区间，市场活跃度提升；水上运输、邮政、互联网软件及信息技术服务等行业商务活动指数均位于55.0%以上较高景气区间，相关企业业务总量增长较快。服务业业务活动预期指数为55.2%，继续位于较高景气区间，多数企业对服务业市场发展保持信心。

10月15日国内成品油价格调整以来，中东地缘紧张局势升级，国际市场原油价格大幅上涨。为减缓对国内的冲击，国家再次对成品油价格采取调控措施。根据现行价格机制计算，自10月29日24时起，国内汽、柴油（标准品）价格每吨分别应上调440元、420元，统筹兼顾减轻下游用户负担和保障成品油安全稳定供应，调控后实际上调345元、335元。
中石油、中石化、中海油公司及其他原油加工企业要组织好成品油生产和调运，确保市场稳定供应，严格执行国家价格政策。各地相关部门要加大市场监督检查力度，严厉查处不执行国家价格政策的行为，维护正常市场秩序。消费者可通过12315平台举报价格违法行为。

据农业农村部监测，2026年第41周（2026年10月5—11日，下同）“农产品批发价格200指数”为114.63（以2015年为100），比前一周降0.50个点，同比低5.79个点。
猪肉批发市场周均价每公斤15.92元，环比跌1.8%，同比低15.5%。
重点监测的28种蔬菜批发市场周均价每公斤4.34元，环比跌0.5%，同比低11.6%。

文章标题
2026年第41周国内猪肉、鸡蛋和蔬菜价格下跌 牛羊肉价格上涨 国际市场食糖价格明显上涨
一、国内鲜活农产品批发价格情况
据农业农村部监测，2026年第41周（2026年10月5—11日，下同）“农产品批发价格200指数”为114.63（以2015年为100），比前一周降0.50个点，同比低5.79个点；“‘菜篮子’产品批发价格指数”为114.75（以2015年为100），比前一周降0.59个点，同比低6.99个点。
1.猪肉、鸡蛋价格环比下跌，牛羊肉价格环比略涨。猪肉批发市场周均价每公斤15.92元，环比跌1.8%，同比低15.5%；牛肉批发市场周均价每公斤72.88元，环比涨0.4%，同比高10.7%；羊肉批发市场周均价每公斤67.58元，环比涨0.1%，同比高9.3%；白条鸡批发市场周均价每公斤17.04元，环比跌0.6%，同比低2.1%。鸡蛋批发市场周均价每公斤10.07元，环比跌3.7%，同比高27.5%。
2.蔬菜均价环比下跌。重点监测的28种蔬菜批发市场周均价每公斤4.34元，环比跌0.5%，同比低11.6%。分品种看，18种蔬菜价格下跌，2种持平，8种上涨。其中，菠菜价格环比跌5.2%，其余品种价格跌幅在5%以内。葱头和大蒜价格环比均基本持平。黄瓜价格环比涨9.1%，其余品种价格涨幅在4%以内。
3.水产品价格环比小幅涨跌。白鲢鱼、鲫鱼、大带鱼、大黄花鱼和草鱼批发市场周均价每公斤分别为9.97元、19.43元、42.29元、48.85元和17.23元，环比分别涨0.7%、涨0.4%、涨0.3%、涨0.2%和涨0.1%。花鲢鱼和鲤鱼批发市场周均价每公斤分别为17.54元和13.89元，环比均跌0.1%。
4.水果均价环比下跌。重点监测的6种水果批发市场周均价每公斤6.63元，环比跌1.5%，同比低6.4%。分品种看，菠萝、富士苹果、巨峰葡萄和香蕉批发市场周均价环比分别跌2.9%、跌2.3%、跌2.2%和跌1.8%。西瓜和鸭梨批发市场周均价环比分别涨2.9%和涨0.8%。
二、国际大宗农产品价格情况
1.食糖价格环比明显上涨，棕榈油价格环比小幅上涨。国际糖料理事会食糖周均价每磅19.87美分（每吨438美元），环比涨10.4%，同比高23.2%。美国芝加哥商品交易所小麦、大豆和豆油连续期货收盘周均价每吨分别为253美元、475美元和1512美元，环比分别涨0.5%、涨0.3%和涨0.8%，同比分别高35.6%、高26.8%和高35.5%。马来西亚棕榈油荷兰鹿特丹港到岸周均价每吨1527美元，环比涨2.0%，同比高12.9%。泰国100%B级和5%破碎率大米曼谷离岸周均价每吨分别为483美元和477美元，环比均涨0.2%，同比分别高29.4%和高33.3%。
2.玉米和棉花价格环比下跌。美国芝加哥商品交易所玉米连续期货收盘周均价每吨196美元，环比跌2.2%，同比高18.7%。国际棉花价格指数（SM级）每磅91.26美分（每吨2012美元），环比跌1.3%，同比高23.2%。

### Kline/Candlestick data
```
GET /api/v3/klines
```
Kline/candlestick bars for a symbol.
Klines are uniquely identified by their open time.
**Weight:**
2
**Parameters:**
Name | Type | Mandatory | Description
------------ | ------------ | ------------ | ------------
symbol | STRING | YES |
interval | ENUM | YES |
startTime | LONG | NO |
endTime | LONG | NO |
timeZone | STRING | NO | Default: 0 (UTC)
limit | INT | NO | Default: 500; Maximum: 1000.
**Data Source:** Database
Supported kline intervals (case-sensitive):
Interval | `interval` value
--------- | ----------------
seconds | `1s`
minutes | `1m`, `3m`, `5m`, `15m`, `30m`
hours | `1h`, `2h`, `4h`, `6h`, `8h`, `12h`
days | `1d`, `3d`
weeks | `1w`
months | `1M`
**Notes:**
* If `startTime` and `endTime` are not sent, the most recent klines are returned.
* Supported values for `timeZone`:
* Hours and minutes (e.g.
`-1:00`, `05:45`)
* Only hours (e.g.
`0`, `8`, `4`)
* Accepted range is strictly [-12:00 to +14:00] inclusive
* If `timeZone` provided, kline intervals are interpreted in that timezone instead of UTC.
* Note that `startTime` and `endTime` are always interpreted in UTC, regardless of `timeZone`.

### Kline/Candlestick data
```

```
Kline/candlestick bars for a symbol.
Klines are uniquely identified by their open time.
**Weight:**
2
**Parameters:**
Name | Type | Mandatory | Description
------------ | ------------ | ------------ | ------------
symbol | STRING | YES |
interval | ENUM | YES |
startTime | LONG | NO |
endTime | LONG | NO |
timeZone | STRING | NO | Default: 0 (UTC)
limit | INT | NO | Default: 500; Maximum: 1000.
**Data Source:** Database
Supported kline intervals (case-sensitive):
Interval | `interval` value
--------- | ----------------
seconds | `1s`
minutes | `1m`, `3m`, `5m`, `15m`, `30m`
hours | `1h`, `2h`, `4h`, `6h`, `8h`, `12h`
days | `1d`, `3d`
weeks | `1w`
months | `1M`
**Notes:**
* If `startTime` and `endTime` are not sent, the most recent klines are returned.
* Supported values for `timeZone`:
* Hours and minutes (e.g.
`-1:00`, `05:45`)
* Only hours (e.g.
`0`, `8`, `4`)
* Accepted range is strictly [-12:00 to +14:00] inclusive
* If `timeZone` provided, kline intervals are interpreted in that timezone instead of UTC.
* Note that `startTime` and `endTime` are always interpreted in UTC, regardless of `timeZone`.

October 28, 2026
Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
For release at 2:00 p.m.
EDT
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:
The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.
While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated.
The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
The Committee will deliver price stability.
Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D.
Cook and Beth M.
Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.
For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955.

Stalled at the Pivot
Binance spot data recorded Ethereum at $2,288.68 at approximately 07:05 UTC on November 2, 2026, a gain of 0.85% over the prior 24 hours within a $2,247.84–$2,317.84 intraday range.
Where that price lands on the chart matters more than the magnitude of the gain: $2,288.68 is barely above the session pivot of $2,284.79, while the 7-day SMA ($2,289.79), EMA 12 ($2,319.73), 20-day SMA ($2,362.49), EMA 26 ($2,387.36), and 50-day SMA ($2,513.46) all sit overhead as resistance.
The one moving average that current price clears is the 200-day SMA at $2,158.70, which it exceeds by roughly $130.
That configuration describes a corrective phase that has not yet cracked the long-term structural floor: ETH is not staging a credible push higher, but it is not breaking down toward that floor either.
It is holding a pivot level it has barely cleared.
A Histogram at Zero
Both the MACD line and signal line registered –67.6364 on Binance spot data as of November 2, placing the histogram at exactly 0.0000.
The gap that had been measuring downside momentum has closed to nothing — the two lines have met.
That is not a reversal signal; it means the bearish momentum has lost its lead over the signal line and the two have drawn level.
In a market where price sits below all short- and medium-term averages, the most supportable reading is a pause within a declining structure rather than a confirmed turn.
Positive histogram prints in subsequent sessions would provide a more credible basis for a constructive view; that evidence is not yet in the supplied data.
The RSI and Stochastic readings from Binance spot data reflect the same suspended state.
The 14-period RSI stood at 36.88 — closer to the oversold threshold of 30 than to the neutral midpoint of 50.
The Stochastic oscillator showed %K at 32.56 crossing above %D at 26.05, a configuration that can precede a short-term lift when it forms in the lower portion of the range, but which carries a high failure rate when the broader price structure is declining.
Taken together with the MACD convergence, the momentum picture is neither confirming further deterioration nor mounting a credible recovery — it is caught between the two.
Bollinger Position and ATR Context

That mean, along with the EMA 26 at $2,387.36, forms a cluster in the $2,362–$2,387 range that would represent the first meaningful structural hurdle if any recovery attempt materialized.
The 14-period ATR of $77.66, also derived from Binance spot daily data, puts the key levels in practical context.
